draft.title: Dominant and recessive alleles
card: an allele that shows in the phenotype when only one copy is present. It is written as a capital letter, such as T.
an allele that shows only when two copies are present. It is written as a lower case letter, such as t.
A Punnett square shows each parent's gametes along the top and side. Each box is a possible offspring genotype, so the boxes give the expected ratios.
A cross of two parents who are both Tt gives TT, Tt, Tt and tt. That is a 3 to 1 ratio of dominant to recessive phenotype, and it is a probability for each offspring, not a guarantee.
draft.remember: A dominant allele shows with one copy. A recessive allele needs two. Punnett squares give the chances.

a.q: In pea plants, tall (T) is dominant to short (t). Which genotype gives a short plant?
a.why: A recessive allele shows only when two copies are present, so a short plant must be tt. Tt is tempting, but the dominant T would show, making the plant tall.
a.clue: A recessive allele needs two copies to show.

b.q: Two tall pea plants, both Tt, are crossed. Tall (T) is dominant to short (t). What is the chance that one offspring is short?
b.why: The Punnett square gives TT, Tt, Tt and tt, and only tt is short, so the chance is 1 in 4. The chance is not 0, because each Tt parent carries a hidden recessive allele that can pass on in the gametes.
b.clue: Draw the square and count the boxes with two recessive alleles.
